It is an [[insect]] of the [[order]] {{taxfmt|Hemiptera|order}}, and so is one of the "true bugs".]] ===Alternative forms=== * {{alter|en|bugg||obsolete}} ===Etymology=== First attested in this form around 1620 (referring to a “[[bedbug]]”), from earlier {{m|en|bugge||beetle}}, from {{der|en|enm|bugge||scarecrow, hobgoblin}} which is traced alternatively to: * a Celtic root found in {{cog|sco|bogill||goblin, bugbear}} and obsolete {{cog|cy|bwg||ghost, hobgoblin}}; compare Welsh {{m|cy|bwgwl||threat, fear}} and {{cog|mga|bocanách||supernatural being}}. * {{der|en|gem-pro|*bugja-||swollen up, thick}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*bʰew-}}, {{m|ine-pro|*bu-||to swell}};{{R:ine:IEW|98-102}} compare {{cog|no|bugge||big man}}, dialectal Low German {{m|nds|Bögge||goblin, snot}}. * or to a word related to {{m|en|buck}} and originally referring to a goat-shaped spectre.{{R:Online Etymology Dictionary|accessdate=12 June 2025}} For the “insect” meaning the assonance with {{der|en|enm|budde||beetle}}, from {{der|en|ang|budda}}, from {{der|en|gmw-pro|*buʀdō}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*buzdô}}, from the same ultimate source as above, might have played a role. Compare {{cog|nds|Budde|t=louse, grub}}, {{cog|no|budda|t=newborn domestic animal}}, {{cog|is|budda|t=purse}}. More at {{l|en|bud}}. But ultimately this convergence of meaning doesn't prove a conflation of the two terms; they might have existed in parallel since PIE times with similar meanings, even if unnoticed by literary sources. Negation of ''let’s'' is ''let’s not'' in standard English.

''Don’t'' is also used, but it is often considered non-standard.
* {{ux|en|'''Let’s don’t''' talk about it.|q=US}}
* {{ux|en|'''Don’t let’s''' talk about it.|q=British}}

Tag questions with ''let’s'' typically take ''shall we?''.
